title: Faith in Words
theme: The root cred: believing and trusting
objectives: I can use the Latin root cred, meaning believe or trust, to work out the meaning of ten words.
I can tell apart look-alike words such as creditable and credible, and credulous and incredulous.
I can judge whether a source deserves trust and explain my decision with words from this unit.
I can write a short argument about trust and evidence using at least four words from this unit.
rationale: Cred is the root behind most of the vocabulary students need to talk about trust: whether a source is believable, whether a speaker is qualified, and how readily a person accepts a claim. The ten words move from the quality of sources (credibility, credentials, accredit, discredit, credence), to the people who read them (credulous, incredulous), to look-alike words that students routinely swap (creditable, incredible, creed). Two pairs are deliberate traps: creditable versus credible, and credulous versus incredulous. The prefixes in-, dis- and ac- and the suffixes -ible, -ity, -ence and -ulous give a second year of word-part practice that transfers to source evaluation in every discipline.

words.def: Good enough to earn praise or respect.
words.ex: The rookie's creditable performance, a close second against the state champion, earned a round of applause.
words.ex2: Eli's creditable effort on the science fair project won second place even though he started late.
words.nonExample: A sloppy report that was finished minutes before the deadline is hardly creditable.

segs.m: praise or recognition given to someone

morph.note: Creditable means able to earn credit, that is, worthy of praise. It is not the same as credible, which means believable.

words.rel: worthy of praise, not of belief

apps.academic: A creditable first draft shows real effort and solid ideas even when it still needs revision.
apps.spoken: That was a creditable score for your first try.
apps.writing: Use creditable for work that earns respect, and credible for a claim that can be believed.

cloze.s: Finishing fourth out of eighty runners was a ___ result for a first-time marathoner.

cloze2.s: Although the film won no awards, critics called the young director's first effort ___ and looked forward to her next one.

misuse.s: The detective called the witness's story creditable because it matched the security footage and the timeline.
misuse.why: A story that can be believed is credible; creditable describes work or effort that deserves praise.

visual.alt: A runner wearing a medal while spectators applaud.

words.frame: A creditable effort is one that ___ even though ___.

words.def: So surprising or impressive that it is hard to believe.
words.ex: The climber described the incredible silence at the summit, where not even the wind stirred.
words.ex2: It is incredible that a single seed can grow into a tree taller than a house.
words.nonExample: An ordinary Tuesday homework assignment is not something anyone would call incredible.

morph.note: In incredible, in- means not, so the word first meant not able to be believed. Today it is used for anything astonishing, good or bad.

apps.academic: A science writer may call a result incredible and then give the data that makes it believable.
apps.spoken: That catch was incredible; I still cannot believe he reached the ball.
apps.writing: Swap a vague incredible for a precise word, such as astonishing or enormous, when you can.

cloze.s: After training for two years, the swimmer broke the school record by an ___ ten seconds, and the crowd gasped.

cloze2.s: The astronomer showed ___ photographs of galaxies so distant that their light began traveling billions of years ago.

misuse.s: The cashier called the change incredible because it was exactly the amount everyone expected.
misuse.why: Incredible describes something astonishing; getting the expected change is ordinary.

visual.alt: A night sky full of glittering stars above a mountain.

words.frame: The most incredible thing I have ever seen is ___ because ___.

words.def: The quality of being trusted, usually because of honesty, knowledge, or a good record.
words.ex: The newspaper lost much of its credibility after it printed three stories that proved false.
words.ex2: A scientist builds credibility by sharing her methods so that others can repeat the work.
words.nonExample: A website with no author, no date, and no named sources has very little credibility.

morph.note: Before -ity the suffix -ible is respelled -ibil- (ible -> ibil), as in credibility and possibility.

words.rel: how much a source is trusted

apps.academic: Evaluating a source means asking whether its author has the credibility to speak on the topic.
apps.spoken: Her credibility took a hit when her story changed.
apps.writing: Tie credibility to evidence: say who the source is and why that person can be trusted.

cloze.s: The reporter's ___ grew each time one of her stories was checked and found accurate.

cloze2.s: The judge doubted the witness's ___ because her account of the night had changed three times.

misuse.s: The website had excellent credibility, so nearly everyone ignored it because no one believed a word it said.
misuse.why: Credibility is the quality of being believed and trusted; a source nobody believes does not have it.

visual.alt: A line from 'not trusted' to 'fully trusted', with credibility near the trusted end.

words.def: Proof of training, experience, or authority to do a job or speak on a subject.
words.ex: Before the hospital hired her, the board checked the surgeon's credentials.
words.ex2: An author's credentials appear at the end of the article so readers can judge whether to trust the claims.
words.nonExample: Having a strong opinion about volcanoes does not give you a volcanologist's credentials.

morph.note: The pieces are shown to spot the pattern. Credentials are the things that give others reason to trust you.

apps.academic: When you analyze a primary source, ask who wrote it and what credentials that person had.
apps.spoken: Before I follow that advice, what are your credentials?
apps.writing: Name a source's credentials in one phrase, such as a marine biologist with twenty years of fieldwork.

cloze.s: The clinic displayed each doctor's ___ on the wall: degrees, licenses, and years of hospital training.

cloze2.s: Her ___ as a certified pilot with ten thousand flight hours made her a trusted voice on the safety panel.

misuse.s: The stranger's credentials as a surgeon were that he was tall and spoke in a loud, confident voice.
misuse.why: Credentials are proof of training or authority, not height or a confident voice.

visual.alt: A framed certificate beside a graduation cap.

words.frame: To judge a speaker's credentials, I would check ___.

words.def: To damage the trust or respect people have for a person, idea, or source.
words.ex: The lawyer tried to discredit the witness by showing that she had changed her story twice.
words.ex2: One faked photograph can discredit an entire news report, even if the rest of it is accurate.
words.nonExample: Praising a coworker's honest work in front of the team builds her reputation instead of discrediting it.

segs.m: belief or trust given to someone

apps.academic: Historians discredit a source when its claims are shown to be false or its author had a reason to lie.
apps.spoken: Do not try to discredit her just because you disagree with her.
apps.writing: Discredit needs an object, so say exactly whom or what the evidence discredits.

cloze.s: The scientists tried to ___ the miracle claim by repeating the experiment and showing that it never worked.

cloze2.s: Rival campaigns sometimes try to ___ each other with rumors instead of facts.

misuse.s: The senator wanted to discredit her opponent, so she praised his honesty and urged every voter to trust him.
misuse.why: To discredit is to damage trust; praising honesty builds trust instead.

visual.alt: A newspaper clipping stamped with a large red X.

words.frame: A source can be discredited if ___.

words.def: Too ready to believe things without enough proof.
words.ex: The credulous shopper believed the ad's claim that one jar of cream would erase every wrinkle in a week.
words.ex2: A credulous reader may share a shocking headline before checking where it came from.
words.nonExample: A person who asks for the original source before sharing a story is not credulous.

morph.note: The suffix -ulous names a habit, here the habit of believing too easily.

apps.academic: Con artists depend on a credulous audience that accepts claims without asking for evidence.
apps.spoken: Do not be so credulous; look it up before you tell everyone.
apps.writing: Credulous is critical in tone; use trusting when you mean a gentler, more positive trait.

cloze.s: The ___ tourist handed his wallet to a stranger who promised to double the money by morning.

cloze2.s: A ___ audience accepted every claim the speaker made, though he offered no proof for any of them.

misuse.s: The credulous detective demanded proof for every claim and doubted every single witness.
misuse.why: Credulous means too ready to believe; demanding proof is the opposite habit.

visual.alt: A fish swimming toward a baited fishing hook.

words.frame: A credulous person might ___ without checking.

words.def: Unwilling or unable to believe something; showing doubt.
words.ex: Mara gave her brother an incredulous look when he said he had cleaned the whole garage in ten minutes.
words.ex2: The judge listened with an incredulous frown as the defendant claimed that a dog had signed the contract.
words.nonExample: A person who nods and accepts every claim at once is not incredulous.

morph.note: Credulous and incredulous differ by only in-, but they point in opposite directions.

apps.academic: A historian may be incredulous at a claim that no document supports.
apps.spoken: I was incredulous when she said she had read the whole book in one night.
apps.writing: Use incredulous for a reaction on a face or in a voice; use incredible for the thing that caused it.

cloze.s: Her eyebrows shot up, and she stared at him with an ___ expression, because no one could finish that puzzle in a minute.

cloze2.s: The driver was ___ when the passengers said they had walked from the airport in the pouring rain.

misuse.s: The incredulous audience accepted the magician's claim at once and clapped without a trace of doubt.
misuse.why: Incredulous means unable or unwilling to believe; accepting a claim without doubt is the opposite.

visual.alt: A person raising one eyebrow while listening to a surprising claim.

words.def: A statement or system of beliefs that guides how a person or group lives.
words.ex: The volunteers' creed, leave every campsite cleaner than you found it, was painted above the cabin door.
words.ex2: People of every race, religion, and creed gathered for the neighborhood festival.
words.nonExample: A snack you happen to like is a preference, not a creed.

apps.academic: A school's creed, such as a motto or honor code, tells students what the community values.
apps.spoken: Her creed is simple: be on time and be kind.
apps.writing: State a creed in one sentence, then show it with a short example of someone acting on it.

cloze.s: The scouts' ___ promises honesty, kindness, and help for anyone in need, and members recite it at every meeting.

cloze2.s: He lived by a simple ___: never make a promise you do not plan to keep.

misuse.s: My creed for lunch today is a turkey sandwich, because I changed my mind three times this morning.
misuse.why: A creed is a lasting set of beliefs that guides a life; a one-day lunch choice is not.

visual.alt: A rolled scroll next to a white dove.

words.def: To officially recognize a school, program, or person as meeting required standards.
words.ex: The state board will accredit the new nursing program only after it inspects the labs and the teachers.
words.ex2: Only reporters accredited by the league may sit in the press box during the game.
words.nonExample: A school that simply calls itself the best in town has not been accredited by anyone.

morph.note: The prefix ad- takes the form ac- before the letter c.

apps.academic: A college's accreditation tells families that outside reviewers have checked its standards.
apps.spoken: Is that program accredited, or is it just advertised?
apps.writing: Accredit needs an authority: a board or agency accredits a school, and a school cannot accredit itself.

cloze.s: Before students can earn a nursing license, the program must be ___ by the state review board.

cloze2.s: The board will ___ the lab only if its equipment, safety record, and teachers all meet the written standards.

misuse.s: The inspectors accredited the clinic even though it had failed every safety test they ran.
misuse.why: To accredit is to approve something as meeting standards; a clinic that failed every test would not be approved.

visual.alt: A school building with a green check mark beside it.

words.frame: A review board might accredit a school if ___.

words.def: Willingness to accept that something is true or likely.
words.ex: The newly found fossil gave credence to the theory that the two continents were once joined.
words.ex2: Few people gave credence to the rumor because no one could say where it began.
words.nonExample: Shrugging off a rumor with no source is a way of withholding credence, not giving it.

apps.academic: Strong evidence lends credence to a hypothesis, while weak evidence does not.
apps.spoken: I do not give much credence to rumors.
apps.writing: Credence usually follows give, lend, or gain: evidence lends credence to a claim.

cloze.s: The matching fingerprints lent ___ to the detective's theory that the thief had entered through the window.

cloze2.s: Because the story came from an anonymous post with no source, few people gave it any ___.

misuse.s: The scientist gave full credence to the claim and refused to accept that it could possibly be true.
misuse.why: To give credence is to accept something as true; refusing to accept it is the opposite.

visual.alt: A line from 'rejected' to 'accepted as true', with credence near the accepted end.

words.frame: I give credence to a claim when ___.

passage.title: The Lighthouse Photo
paras: On Monday morning a photograph raced through the eighth-grade group chat: a lighthouse glowing violet beneath a sky split by lightning, captioned “Taken last night at Harbor Point.” Nearly everyone called the picture incredible. Priya, the editor of the school newspaper, was not so sure.

“A credulous editor would print it and move on,” she told her reporter, Marcus. “First we find out who took it.” The post carried no name, and the account that shared it had been created that very morning. That alone weakened its credibility.

Marcus began searching. He learned that the photograph had been posted two years earlier by a photographer in another country, long before any storm at Harbor Point. Then he telephoned Ms. Alvarez, the lighthouse keeper, whose credentials were hard to question: thirty years of tending the light and a coast guard certificate framed in her office. “We had no lightning here last night,” she said. “The sky stayed clear until midnight.”

Priya was incredulous that so many classmates had shared the image without a second thought. “One fake can discredit a whole feed,” Marcus said, “and people will stop believing the real pictures too.” Priya did not want to lecture anyone. She wanted readers to watch the check happen, so the next issue explained each step: find the original source, look at the poster's record, and ask someone who actually knows the place.

The principal praised the feature as a creditable piece of student journalism. The journalism program, which an outside board had recently accredited, pinned it to the wall as a model. Beside it Priya hung the staff's creed, written on an index card: Print only what we can prove. She hoped that the next time a shocking picture arrived, her classmates would give it credence only after it had passed the same test.

qs.q: In paragraph 2, the word “credulous” most nearly means
choices: eager to publish before other newspapers
careful about checking every fact
too ready to believe something without proof
angry at classmates who posted the picture
qs.why: Priya says a credulous editor would print the picture and move on, so the word describes someone who accepts a claim without checking it.

qs.q: Why does the age of the account weaken the post's credibility?
choices: A brand-new account with no name gives readers no record to trust.
The school forbids anyone from posting photographs.
The account belonged to a student at Priya's school.
Priya dislikes pictures that are posted in the morning.
qs.why: Credibility depends on a track record. An account created that very morning has none, and it names no photographer.

qs.q: Which detail best shows that Ms. Alvarez's testimony deserves trust?
choices: She said there had been no lightning last night.
She answered when Marcus telephoned her.
She works in an office near the harbor.
She has kept the light for thirty years and holds a coast guard certificate.
qs.why: Her long experience and her certificate are credentials, the proof that she is qualified to speak about Harbor Point.

qs.q: What does Priya's reaction in paragraph 4 show about her?
choices: She believes the real pictures are less interesting.
She is surprised that many classmates accepted the picture without checking it.
She plans to punish students who shared the image.
She is certain that nobody will believe the newspaper again.
qs.why: Incredulous means unable to believe, and she cannot believe how many people shared the picture without a second thought. She chooses to teach rather than lecture.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses a central idea of the passage?
choices: Photographs of storms are almost always fake.
Student newspapers should avoid anything found online.
A claim deserves belief only after its source has been checked.
Lighthouse keepers are the best source on any topic.
qs.why: Priya's whole plan, from the staff creed to the three-step check, is to give belief only to what has been verified.

write.prompt: Describe a time you checked whether a claim, rumor, or picture could be trusted. Use at least three words from this unit to explain what you looked for and what you decided.
write.frame: I questioned the ___ because ___, so I checked ___ and decided ___.

study.task: Build a family tree for cred: put the root at the top and add at least five words from the unit, each with the prefix or suffix that changes it. Under each word write a short meaning, then circle the two pairs that are easy to confuse and explain how a word part keeps them apart.

sentences: Write a sentence about a source you would trust and name two credentials that earn that trust.
Write a sentence that uses both credulous and evidence to describe someone who accepts too much too fast.
Write a sentence in which a rumor loses all credence. Say why.
Write a sentence that uses creditable for a performance that was not first place but still earned respect.

combine.model: Because the website listed no author and cited no sources, its credibility was low and readers doubted it.

given: The lawyer found a lie in the witness's story.
She used it against the witness.
combine.model: The lawyer found a lie in the witness's story and used it to discredit the witness.

discuss: Is it better to be a little credulous or a little incredulous? Use both words and give an example.
Can a person with weak credentials still be right? How should a reader treat that person's claim?
Why might an accredited school or program be trusted more than one that is not? What does accreditation not guarantee?
produce.explain: Explain the difference between creditable and credible. Use both words in one clear example about a student project.

argue.prompt: Claim: Every student should be required to check the credibility of a source before using it in a school assignment. Take a side and support it with two reasons that use words from this unit.
argue.frame: I believe that ___ because ___. A source with strong credentials would ___, but a credulous reader would ___.

constructed.prompt: A classmate quotes an article about a medical treatment. Write what you would ask about the author before trusting the article. Use credibility and credentials, and explain why those questions matter.
look: asks about the author's training or record
explains why trust should depend on evidence about the source
constructed.model: I would ask what credentials the author has, such as medical training or years of research. If the author has none, the article has little credibility, because nothing shows the author knows enough to be believed.

constructed.prompt: Describe two people who hear the same surprising claim, one credulous and one incredulous. Use both words and show each reaction with an action.
look: gives a concrete action for each reaction
shows that the two reactions are opposites
constructed.model: When the ad promised instant fluency in a week, the credulous buyer paid at once. The incredulous one raised an eyebrow, read the fine print, and walked away.

constructed.prompt: Explain how a lie found in one part of a story can change how much credence people give to the rest of it. Use discredit and credence.
look: links one proven falsehood to doubt about other claims
keeps the cause and effect clear
constructed.model: Once reporters discredit one part of a story by proving it false, readers give less credence to every other claim in it, because they no longer know which parts to trust.

teacher.overview: Students use the Latin root cred to build and sort ten words about trust, practice two confusable pairs, and apply the vocabulary to a short narrative about checking a viral photograph. The unit pairs word-part work with source evaluation, so it connects to earlier work on bias and testimony and to the technology and argument units later in the year.

notes.va.creditable.adj: The headline trap of the unit: creditable (worthy of praise) is not credible (believable). Put both on the board with a sentence each. A quick check: you can give credit to a creditable performance, and you can believe a credible witness.
notes.va.incredible.adj: Incredible began as not able to be believed and now usually means astonishing. Students will use it as a vague superlative; ask them to replace it with a more exact word. Show that the in- here means not, unlike the in- in words such as inside.
notes.va.credibility.n: Credibility is the noun for how far a source can be trusted. Have students rate three sources (a lab report, an anonymous post, a textbook) and name what raised or lowered each one. Notice the spelling shift from -ible to -ibil- before -ity.
notes.va.credentials.n: Credentials are proof of training or authority, and they are not the same as popularity or confidence. Ask which credentials matter for which topic: a pilot's credentials do not make her an expert on nutrition. The word is almost always plural.
notes.va.discredit.v: Discredit is about damaging trust, whether fairly (exposing a real lie) or unfairly (a smear). Ask students to decide which of two scenarios is fair. The base is credit, so dis- reverses the trust given.
notes.va.credulous.adj: Credulous carries a mild criticism: it means too ready to believe. Contrast with trusting (neutral to positive) and skeptical (the opposite habit). Model the suffix -ulous as a tendency or habit.
notes.va.incredulous.adj: Credulous and incredulous differ by in-, and the in- means not. Students often reverse them. Use faces: the credulous person nods at once; the incredulous person raises an eyebrow. The speaker or listener is incredulous; the claim is incredible.
notes.va.creed.n: A creed is a set of beliefs that guides how someone lives, and it is not limited to religion: a team, a school, or a profession can have one. The word shares its Latin source (credo, I believe) with the cred words, which is worth a mention. Ask students to write a creed in one sentence.
notes.va.accredit.v: Accredit means an outside authority approves something as meeting standards. Students may think any school can accredit itself; stress the outside board. Link to credentials: a person has credentials, and a program is accredited.
notes.va.credence.n: Credence is acceptance of a claim as true, and it usually appears in phrases such as give credence to or lend credence to. A fact lends credence; a listener gives it. Have students rewrite three sentences that use believe with credence.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: “The post has no name and the account is a day old. I am not going to be credulous. Before I give it any credence, I want the original source. The keeper has thirty years of experience and a certificate, so her credentials give her credibility on this question. If the photo came from another year, it is discredited, and the post is not just unproven but false.”
discuss: What is the difference between a source being credible and a performance being creditable?
Where is the line between being incredulous and being cynical about everything?
How much do credentials matter when the claim is easy to check yourself?
misconceptions: Creditable and credible mean the same thing.
Incredulous and incredible both describe the surprising thing.
Credulous is a compliment meaning trusting and kind.
Anyone with strong opinions has credentials.
extend: Collect three real news corrections and decide what each one did to the outlet's credibility.
Write a one-sentence personal creed and a short scene in which a character acts on it.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit credible versus creditable and credulous versus incredulous after two days with a quick sort, again at one week using real headlines, and weave credibility, credentials and discredit into the technology unit's discussion of misinformation.

frames: I would trust the source because the author has ___ credentials such as ___.
I was incredulous when ___, but a credulous person would have ___.
wida.oral: Partner A reads a surprising claim aloud. Partner B reacts as a credulous person and then as an incredulous person, using the words, and both partners decide what evidence they would ask for.
